newsitem.title: UK: Dollar better bid in Europe after post-G7 fall.
newsitem.headline: Dollar better bid in Europe after post-G7 fall.

text.p: The dollar was bid in early European trading after sliding quite sharply in the Far East in the wake of Saturday's G7 meeting, and many still see it going higher.
The market was long going into the meeting and the overnight shakeout reflected little more than some of those longs being cleared out, dealers said.
"It is very well bid this morning," said Nick Parsons, currency strategist at Banque Paribas. "I don't think the market is going to give this up at the first attempt."

The official statement issued by the seven nations said "We discussed the developments on currency and financial markets. We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets, noted in our April 1995 communique, have been corrected."
There was no talk of intervention, concerted or unilateral, and economic fundamentals still argue for a firmer dollar.

"Whatever G7 wish, they can't wish away the interest rate differential, they can't wish away the growth cycles and they can't wish away the generally more favourable attitude for U.S. assets," Paribas' Parsons said.

The dollar dipped to 1.6350 marks and 120.40 yen overnight in the immediate aftermath of the meeting statement but by 0827 GMT it had clawed back two pfennigs to 1.6550 and nearly three yen to 123.30.

Dollar/mark is seen having more upside potential than dollar/yen given that of the G7 nations, Japan is the most worried about the weakness of its currency versus the dollar and the most likely to intervene.
Japan's external reserves stood at $217 billion in January so it has plenty of ammunition. "If you play dollar/yen you could well find the BoJ is the counter-party," said one dealer.
